posts.cooked:
The reasons Blizzard gave for banning GDKP in Season of Discovery simply do not apply to TBC Anniversary and the justifications they pivoted to afterward are contradicted by actual player experience.

Let’s break it down cleanly.

1. Blizzard’s original justification was RMT and it didn’t work

Blizzard’s first stated reason for banning GDKP was that it created artificial gold demand that encouraged RMT and botting. Their own words:

GDKP in Season of Discovery

It’s also undeniable that GDKP contributes to and drives a lot of illicit activity, such as real-money trading (RMT) and botting, as it creates a demand for in-game gold that would not otherwise exist. GDKP can create an “arms race” effect that encourages participating players to purchase gold to be able to compete for the best items.

But as players immediately pointed out -

“Blizz thought banning them would have some impact on RMT and bots… have you noticed less people buying gold? Noticed any reduction in bots?”

The ban did not reduce RMT.
It did not reduce botting.
It did not reduce gold inflation.

So Blizzard quietly shifted to a new justification.

2. Blizzard’s second justification “GDKP erodes guild and social structures” is factually wrong

Their next claim was:

GDKP in Season of Discovery

GDKP erodes traditional guild and social structures that are in many cases the basis of our most fond memories of early versions of World of Warcraft.

This is the argument they fell back on after the RMT justification failed to produce results.

But this claim doesn’t match reality especially not in TBC.

In TBC, GDKP actually strengthened guilds:

  • Guilds had more geared alts available.

  • Players could swap characters in and out when someone called out.

  • Guild raids became more stable because members had multiple viable characters.

  • GDKP runs acted as supplemental gearing pipelines for guilds.

  • Guilds didn’t lose members they gained flexibility.

The OP in your tab even points out that guilds are unchanged:

Waterflaps:

Guild are still guilds, nothing has changed there.

The “social erosion” argument is a retroactive justification, not a real phenomenon.

3. TBC Anniversary is not SoD the environments are completely different

SoD is:

  • seasonal

  • experimental

  • accelerated

  • intentionally restrictive

TBC Anniversary is:

  • stable

  • long‑form

  • progression‑driven

  • built around gearing alts and maintaining raid rosters

The economic and social conditions Blizzard cited simply do not exist in TBC Anniversary.

GDKP fits TBC.
GDKP does not fit SoD.
Blizzard’s own logic supports this distinction.

4. GDKP solves problems that MS/OS and SR raids create

The OP lays this out clearly:

  • SR raids are toxic

  • People leave when their SR doesn’t drop

  • No commitment

  • Wasted time

  • Inflation is worse

  • RMT is worse

  • Guilds are unchanged

All of this is visible in the tab you’re viewing.
GDKP fixes these issues by:

  • eliminating loot drama

  • rewarding participation

  • stabilizing pug culture

  • keeping raids alive late‑phase

  • giving geared players a reason to keep raiding

  • providing guilds with more geared alts

GDKP is not the problem it’s the solution.

5. Removing GDKP didn’t stop RMT it just removed transparency

With GDKP gone, RMT didn’t disappear. It just moved into whispers, guild deals, and under‑the‑table trades.

GDKP payouts are visible, logged, and auditable.
Non‑GDKP loot systems are opaque.

If Blizzard actually wants to fight RMT, GDKP is easier to monitor than the alternatives.

TLDR:

Blizzard banned GDKP in SoD/TBC Anni for reasons that have been disproven. Their RMT justification failed, their “guild erosion” justification doesn’t match reality, and the actual player experience shows that GDKP strengthens raid stability, guild flexibility, and overall game health. Bringing GDKP back to TBC Anniversary isn’t just reasonable it’s the option that best supports the game’s long‑term raiding ecosystem.

I would like to see GDKPs return. In my experience they actually promote pro-social activity, because you get to know people by running repeatedly, and across guilds. People make and gear alts specifically to get more raid lockouts, meaning you get more opportunities to raid with them, meaning you get to know them better.

I understand that people don’t want loot to become pay to win. I agree with that completely. But GDKPs are not a pay to win system. At the end of a GDKP, you get paid just for joining the raid. It’s just like DKP, where you earn points for killing bosses, but those points can be transferred to another raid or used to buy materials. If you don’t have enough gold to buy gear, just do more raids and pretty soon you’ll have plenty. Roll a toon for a role that’s in demand (healers are always in demand!) and find a raid leader who will give you an extra percentage for healing.

Also, you know how it’s frustrating that people will raid until they have the gear they need and then stop raiding with that toon until a new phase drops and they need new gear? And you’re always raiding with toons that aren’t fully geared, or who don’t know what they’re doing? GDKP fixes that. It creates an incentive to continue running raids even if you don’t need anything from it – especially if you don’t need anything from it, because then it’s pure profit for you.

I know there are a lot of objections to GDKPs but I think most of them are just misinformed. The only real one is that it may drive people to buy gold instead of earning it. But that’s not a GDKP problem, people are buying gold anyway. And (as I said before) GDKPs are the best way I know of to earn gold honestly and consistently.
